title: Value Ranked K From the Top
statement:
You get an integer array nums and an integer k. Return the value that would be at position k if nums were sorted from largest to smallest (position 1 is the largest).

Duplicates each take their own position: this is the k-th largest value counting copies, not the k-th largest distinct value. Try to beat a full sort.

examples.why: Sorted from the top: 8, 8, 5, 3. Both 8s take a position, so position 2 is still 8. Counting distinct values would give 5.
From the top: 9, 7, 4, 4, 1. Position 3 is the first 4.
k equal to the length asks for the smallest value.

hints: Sorting answers it in O(n log n). If k is small, do you really need the order of every element?
Keep only the k largest values seen so far. Which of those k is the answer, and which one gets pushed out when a bigger value arrives? A min-heap of size k does exactly that.
For average O(n): partition around a random pivot into larger, equal and smaller groups. The counts tell you which group holds position k, so you only continue into that one group.

explain.intuition:
Heap: keep a min-heap of the k largest values seen so far. Its root is the smallest of those k, which is exactly the k-th largest. A new value that beats the root pushes the root out. After the scan, the root is the answer. This costs O(n log k) and only O(k) memory, so it also works on a stream.

Quickselect: quicksort without the second half. Pick a pivot and split the values into those greater than it, equal to it and less than it. If position k falls among the greater ones, recurse there; if it falls among the equal ones, the pivot is the answer; otherwise recurse into the smaller ones with k reduced. Each round drops one side completely, so on average the work is n + n/2 + n/4 + … ≈ 2n, O(n). The worst case is O(n²): a pivot that is always the largest or smallest shrinks the range by one element per round. A random pivot makes that vanishingly unlikely for any input. The three-way split matters too: with a two-way split, an array of 100 000 equal values never shrinks, because every value lands on the same side as the pivot.
steps: Heap version: push each value into a min-heap; when its size exceeds k, pop the root. Return the root at the end.
Quickselect version: pick a random pivot p from the current values.
Count or collect the values > p (call that group G) and the values equal to p (E).
If k ≤ |G|, continue with G. Else if k ≤ |G| + |E|, return p.
Else continue with the values < p and k − |G| − |E|.
pitfalls: Removing duplicates first, or counting distinct values. Example 1 then answers 5 instead of 8.
Quickselect with a fixed pivot such as the first element. On sorted or reverse-sorted input every round removes one element: O(n²).
A two-way partition (≤ p and > p). With many equal values the range barely shrinks and it degrades to O(n²) even with a random pivot.

complexity.time: O(n log k) with a heap; O(n) average with quickselect
complexity.space: O(k) with a heap; O(1) extra for in-place quickselect

solutions.title: Sort and index
solutions.idea: Sort in descending order and return the value at index k − 1. Simple and fast enough, but does more work than needed.

solutions.title: Min-heap of size k
solutions.idea: Keep the k largest values in a min-heap. The root is the smallest of them, which is the k-th largest overall.

solutions.title: Quickselect with a random pivot
solutions.idea: Partition around a random pivot into greater, equal and smaller groups, then continue only into the group that holds position k.
solutions.space: O(1) extra in TypeScript (in place), O(n) in the Python version
